subtitle: Crusty Mexican rolls
story: Mexico's everyday bread: crackly crust, soft inside, pointed at both ends. It's for molletes, tortas, capirotada and dunking in caldo. Grandmas also say a bite of bolillo calms a scare. It came out of French baking during the Intervention of the 1860s. In Guadalajara its cousin is the birote salado, slightly sour and firm-crusted: the bread of the torta ahogada.
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt. Add the water and lard and mix into a dough.
Knead 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and let rise 1–1½ hours, until doubled.
Divide into [[10 pieces]] (about 85 g). Flatten each into an oval, then roll it up tightly from a long side into a log, pressing the seam closed.
Roll the ends under your palms so they taper to points. Set seam side down on a lined sheet pan.
Cover and let rise 45 minutes, until puffy.
Heat the oven to 425°F with an empty pan on the bottom rack. Slash each roll once down the length, about ¼ inch deep.
Spray or brush the rolls with water. Put them in the oven and pour a cup of hot water into the empty pan for steam. Close the door fast.
Bake 20–25 minutes, until golden and they sound hollow when you tap the bottom. Cool on a rack.
pressureNote: No pressure-cooker version. Bread needs the oven, and steam in the oven is what makes the crust crackle.
tips: The steam is the secret to the thin, crackly crust. Don't skip the pan of water.
Day-old bolillos are perfect for molletes and capirotada.

variations.name: Teleras
variations.subtitle: Flat torta rolls
variations.note: The soft, flat roll for tortas, with two grooves across the top.
steps: Divide the dough into [[8 pieces]] and shape into flat ovals about ¾ inch thick.
Press two deep lines along the length of each with the handle of a wooden spoon, almost to the bottom.
Rise 45 minutes and bake at 400°F for 18–20 minutes, without steam, so the crust stays soft.
